summary: A joke RFC published on April 1 that pretends to define a Telnet option for displaying subliminal messages. It is humor and not a real protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This is an April 1 joke document. It pretends to define a Telnet option that flashes messages on a terminal to persuade users to upgrade their software.

subtitle: An April 1 joke proposing that Telnet display subliminal messages.

tldr.problem: The RFC jokes that some users continue using older Telnet versions despite messages and newsletters encouraging upgrades.
tldr.mechanism: It pretends to define a SUBLIMINAL-MESSAGE option that negotiates permission and sends a message with display duration and frequency values.
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1 joke document, not a real Telnet feature specification.

today: RFC 1097 is an April 1 joke document that pretends to specify a Telnet subliminal-message option. Its stated default is that messages are not displayed.

sections.title: The SUBLIMINAL-MESSAGE Option
sections.content:
RFC 1097 is dated 1 April 1989 and gives a fictional Telnet option the name SUBLIMINAL-MESSAGE and code 257. The memo presents the option as a way to request permission to display subliminal messages.

Its motivation jokes that banners and newsletters may not persuade some users to upgrade an old Telnet version.
sections.plainLanguage: This is an April 1 joke. It proposes hidden terminal messages as a way to persuade people to upgrade Telnet.

sections.title: Negotiating and Sending a Message
sections.content:
The option uses the Telnet WILL, WONT, DO, and DONT commands to negotiate whether subliminal messages may be displayed. A subnegotiation carries a 16-bit duration in milliseconds, a 16-bit frequency in seconds, and the message string.

The default is WONT and DONT, so messages are not displayed unless the option is negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: The fictional option first uses Telnet commands to negotiate permission. It then sends display duration, the interval between displays, and the message.

sections.title: Examples in the RFC
sections.content:
The examples show a server negotiating the option and sending “Use VMS,” then replacing that message with “Go home.” A later empty message stops the display.

The implementation notes joke about placing messages at the edge of the user's visual field and about displaying Morse code on a keyboard caps-lock LED.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples send a message, replace it, and then stop displaying it. The implementation notes continue the RFC's humorous premise.
